title: Patch clamp recording from bipolar cells in the wholemount mouse retina
protocol: Euthanize a mouse with CO2 gas in dark conditions.
Increase the CO2 flow rate to its maximum once the mouse stops moving.
Confirm unresponsiveness of the mouse by pinching the tail and performing cervical dislocation using hemostats.
Enucleate the eyes using #5/45 Dumont forceps and place them in a 35 mm dish filled with oxygenated HEPES solution.
Transfer the dish with eyes into an oxygenated dark box immediately after enucleation.
Place one eye in the dissection chamber under a stereo microscope, filled with HEPES solution continuously oxygenated.
Make a cut on the cornea using a small surgical knife.
Cut the cornea down to the sclera using a pair of Vannas scissors.
Make a circumferential cut around the cornea to remove the iris and cornea on the sclera just above the extraocular muscle attachment.
Remove the lens from the eyecup using #55 forceps.
Pour fresh oxygenated HEPES solution into the eyecup using a 1 mL transfer pipette.
Place this eye back in the dark box.
Remove the other eye and complete steps e-f on the new eye.
Carry out the rest of the dissection on this more recently removed eye.
Remove the transparent vitreous humor from the surface of the retina using sharp forceps.
Grab near the surface of the retina and pull the vitreous away carefully.
Target the ora serrata initially to efficiently remove the vitreous.
Make a small cut on the edge of the retina to mark the side for experimental use.
Detach the retina from the sclera using two pairs of forceps; hold the sclera with one and scrape off the retinal tissue by the other.
Isolate the retina from the eyecup by pinching the optic nerve head with forceps.
Cut and trim the retina into four sections.
Transfer a piece of tissue onto a coverslip with grease rails in a 35 mm dish with HEPES solution using a large transfer pipette.
Position the tissue between the rails with the ganglion cell side up.
Grab the horseshoe net using #5 forceps and place the net over the tissue.
Place the dish in the oxygenated dark box.
Take a wholemount retina from the dark box and place it in the recording chamber on the patch clamp microscope stage.
Start Ames’ solution perfusion at a rate of 3–5 mL per minute using a gravity fed perfusion setup.
Set the temperature to 33 degrees Celsius.
Place a 3 M KCl agar bridge onto a reference wire for the micro pipette before mounting the retinal tissue.
Alternatively, use a permanent silver chloride wire.
Using the 10× objective, place the retinal tissue in the viewing area.
Put a recording pipette in the pipette holder on a micromanipulator.
Advance the tip of the pipette into the center of the viewing area.
Slowly move the pipette down into the Ames’ solution.
Change to a 60× objective.
Under the 60× objective, slowly lower the lens until you find the pipette tip.
Lower the objective focus and the pipette tip in a back and forth manner repeatedly, until the tip is approximately 200 μm above the tissue.
Apply positive pressure into the pipette by inflating it with 1 mL of air for wholemount tissue recordings.
Mix 15 mM sterile HCl to reconstitute human recombinant leptin.
Apply positive pressure into the pipette to prevent clogging from tissue and vitreous.
Set the pipette current to zero using the Axoclamp 700B commander.
Start the Membrane Test program on the Clampex to measure the pipette resistance.
Penetrate the inner limiting membrane (ILM) with the pipette tip.
Advance the pipette tip to the tissue and penetrate the ILM, observing the separation of the membrane and ganglion cells.
Advance the pipette further horizontally and slightly deeper if it does not separate the membrane and ganglion cells.
Check for pipette pressure leaks or tissue tension issues if separation is still not achieved.
Approach the inner nuclear layer (INL) obliquely with the pipette.
Position the pipette on a bipolar cell soma where the edge is clearly visible.
Advance the pipette slowly until a slight dimple on the cell membrane is observed.
Release positive pressure after observing the dimple.
Increase pipette resistance on the Membrane Test slowly to 100 MΩ.
Apply a small amount of negative pressure if resistance does not increase.
Switch the Membrane Test program from Bath mode (Holding potential, 0 mV) to Cell Attached mode (-70 mV).
Wait until the resistance becomes above 1 GΩ to achieve the giga-seal.
Apply a small amount of negative pressure to rupture the membrane within the pipette if necessary.
Use a 50–100 μs zap to rupture the membrane if negative pressure is not sufficient.
Switch the Membrane Test to Cell mode once the membrane ruptures.
Wait for approximately 3 minutes for the intracellular solution to stabilize the recording.
Apply a small negative pressure to the pipette if the baseline current becomes more negative than -100 pA.
Remove and replace the pipette if applying negative pressure does not improve the baseline current.
Check the sulforhodamine image of the bipolar cell after establishing whole-cell configuration.
Use an area of retina where tissue was previously penetrated for a second pipette insertion.
Record the light-evoked postsynaptic currents (L-EPSCs) in control Ames’ solution.
Switch to voltage-clamp mode for tissue illumination with background green light.
Illuminate the tissue with a ∼150 μm spot of light using a 500 nm LED.
Increase the light level to 1.0 × 10^7 photons/μm²/s for one second.
Check if the bipolar cell responds as ON, OFF, or shows no response.
If no light response is present, examine the cell morphology and move on to another cell.
Record several L-EPSCs when the cell responds to light stimulation.
Start perfusion of Ames’ solution containing glutamate receptor blockers.
Run the same light stimulation protocol after blocker perfusion for recording L-EPSCs.
Expect no L-EPSCs due to blocked glutamate receptors and insufficient ChR2 activation.
If a light response persists, wait additional minutes before recording L-EPSCs again.
Increase the stimulus light level to activate ChR2.
Record L-EPSCs in the absence or presence of nicotinic acetylcholine antagonists, MLA and HEX.
Add MLA or HEX to perfusing Ames’ solution with glutamate receptor blockers.
Perfuse the first cholinergic blocker for over 5 minutes.
Record several L-EPSCs after perfusion.
If the first blocker does not affect the L-EPSCs, apply the second cholinergic blocker in addition to the first drug.
Wash out the first drug with Ames’ solution if a change is observed after its application.
Perfuse the second cholinergic blocker for 5 minutes.
Record ChR2-evoked EPSCs after perfusion of the second blocker.
Wash out the drug solution with regular Ames’ solution.
Determine if normal photoreceptor light response is present.
Image terminals of recorded cell to determine bipolar cell type.
Image your cell using epifluorescence for sulforhodamine and ChR2-EYFP fluorescence.
Visualize the sulforodamine in the recording pipette and the soma of the recorded cell.
Use the rhodamine (red) fluorescence cube and the bright LED light (∼560 nm).
Identify bipolar cells.
View deeper into the tissue to find the dendrites of the cell after viewing the pipette and connected soma.
Check that the dendrites go down to the OPL and have some branches.
Search toward the surface of the tissue to view the terminals of the bipolar cell if no dendrites are present, indicating an amacrine cell recording.
Identify a single axon shaft emerging from the soma.
Observe the axon spreading out to terminals in the IPL.
Observe the YFP expression with a GFP filter cube via 500 nm LED light illumination with the CoolLED.
Compare the location of the axon terminals ramification and the ON and OFF ChAT bands.
Capture images of YFP at the same depth as that of the terminals.
